title: As for me and my house (Joshua 24:15)
hookLine: choose this day whom you'll serve

lines: A PLAQUE BY THE FRONT DOOR.
cards: A plaque by a front door, or letters over a kitchen archway: as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. There it reads like a household motto.
But the line was first said by an old soldier at a tense public assembly, in front of every tribe of Israel, and it was a dare. Joshua is near the end of his life. The land has been settled.
And he calls everyone to a town called Shechem, to make them choose.

teach.h: A LAND YOU DIDN'T WORK FOR.
teach.b: First, Joshua retells the whole story, speaking for God: Abraham called from beyond the river, Jacob going down to Egypt, Moses and Aaron, the sea, the wilderness, a land you didn't work for, cities you didn't build, vineyards you didn't plant.
Everything you have was given. Second, the choice.

teach.h: CHOOSE THIS DAY WHOM YOU'LL SERVE.
teach.b: If serving the Lord seems wrong to you, choose this day whom you will serve: the old gods your ancestors served, or the gods of the land you're living in.
Then his own answer, before anyone else's: "but as for me and my house we will serve the Lord." He goes first, and he answers for his household, not the whole nation. Third, the surprise.
The people shout: we'll serve the Lord too! And Joshua says something no one expects.
You can't. He is a holy God, a jealous God. It's as if he wants them to feel the weight of it, not just say yes because everyone else is.
They say it again: no, we will serve the Lord.
So he writes it down and sets up a great stone under an oak as a witness. Fourth, look back over the road. It began with two midwives who said no.

Then a basket in the reeds, a bush that burned, a lamb and a sea, manna, Sinai and ten words, a golden calf, God's back, a blessing, a talking donkey, the Shema, choose life, Moses on Nebo, Rahab's cord.
And it ends where Moses ended: with a choice that has to be made again. At Easter, the Church asks Catholics to make it again, renewing their baptismal promises out loud.

how: At the Easter Vigil and on Easter Sunday, Catholics renew their baptismal promises aloud, rejecting sin and professing faith, and many Catholic families call their home a domestic church, a phrase the Catechism uses for the Christian household.

o: the city whose walls fell when the trumpets blew
the town where Joshua made Israel choose whom to serve
the mountain where Moses received the ten words

games.q: what's inside the day at Shechem — tap the pairs.
p: set up under an oak as witness

s: as for me and my house was first written as a household motto
it was Joshua's answer at a public assembly of all Israel, a dare to choose.
Joshua told the people they couldn't serve the Lord
he is a holy God, Joshua says. the people insist, and choose again.
Joshua answered for the whole nation
he answered for himself and his household, then asked the people to choose.

games.q: you're Joshua at Shechem. you've told the whole story and asked the people to choose. they shout back: we'll serve the Lord too! what do you say?
o: you can't serve the Lord. he is a holy God.
games.why: he tells them they can't, because God is holy. he wants them to feel the weight. they insist, and he sets up a stone as a witness.

practice: Bring one of your big choices to mind: a faith, a marriage, a vocation, staying sober, a promise to a friend. Israel had said yes at Sinai, and Joshua still asked again; if you can, choose yours again, freshly, for today.
If you pray, make Joshua's line your own; if not, renew it in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Shechem. The town where Joshua answered first, for his own household, and dared the people to choose too. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I and my house. the start of Joshua's answer in Joshua 24:15.

carryVoice: Your line: we will serve the lord. Tomorrow, new country: judges, kings, prophets, wisdom, and the seven books. Day three hundred ninety-one, done.

sources.q: but as for me and my house we will serve the Lord.
